story.name: Upholding women's sexual and reproductive health and rights for health equity

content.title: Upholding women's sexual and reproductive health and rights for health equity
content.author: Professor Marleen Temmerman

content.text: The highest attainable standard of health is a fundamental right of every human being.  However, just like the pursuit of gender equity, health equity remains a challenge. The health and wellbeing of women and girls globally continues to be shaped by social dynamics which hinder the enjoyment of this right. The sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) of women and girls has particularly been disregarded when health systems are overwhelmed during health emergencies. There is, nonetheless, growing opportunities to enhance equal access to quality sexual and reproductive health (SRH) services.

The COVID-19 pandemic drew attention to the high risks that women face during pandemics thus showing a dire need for better responses during emergency situations. The measures put in place to prevent the spread of the pandemic, among other factors such as curfews, restriction of movement and reduction in numbers of patients allowed in facilities, created a deficiency in the provision of some crucial health services, including SRH services. Experience from the Zika and Ebola outbreaks also established that there were severe disruptions to SRH services which ultimately exposed women and girls to health risks that were otherwise preventable.
A 2022 study by the African Population and Health Research Centre (APHRC) on the
Impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on sexual and reproductive health services

reported that women and girls had limited access to critical SRH services - contraceptive services, antenatal care, post-abortion care (PAC), and HIV/AIDS prevention and management - during the pandemic. The report stated that over a quarter of women and girls who needed various modern contraceptives could not access them. Consequently, the severe disruptions in SRH services translated to negative experiences and outcomes for women and girls.

Aga Khan University's Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health, East Africa (CoEWCH EA), in collaboration with the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), examined the potential ways that Kenya's COVID-19 control measures affected the SRHR of low resource communities with a focus on women of reproductive age (15-49 years) and female adolescents (15-19 years). The study,
Impact of COVID-19 mitigation measures in Kenya on reproductive health: case of Nairobi, Kilifi and Mombasa counties
, aimed to learn from this pandemic to contribute to better preparedness for future public health crises.

As indicated by the study, less women sought sexual reproductive health services and sexual and gender-based violence (SGBV) escalated once the mitigation measures were implemented. Cases of SGBV continued to increase throughout the course of the pandemic. The study recommended the use of long-term family planning methods during pandemics as an intervention to prevent the consequences of limited access to SRH services. Additionally, it suggested inventing and implementing effective ways to not only report and record SGBV cases but also intervene through community-based programmes and by taking advantage of mobile technology to report and intervene in cases of SGBV.
The International Day of Action for Women's Health, under the theme
"Our Voices, Our Actions, Our Demand: Uphold Women's Health and Rights Now!"

highlights that an attack on SRHR anywhere attacks all our rights everywhere. Prioritising other emergency responses during public health crises at the expense of SRH services solves one problem while creating another. There ought to be coordinated action to establish a balance of health responses so that demands are met to maintain essential health service delivery. Every woman and girl is entitled to equitable access to quality SRH services at all times to prevent adverse outcomes. Therefore, the provision of comprehensive SRHR interventions for all populations throughout is critical in the global efforts to realise health equity.
